Most theory books say that Western music runs on two systems, **major** and **minor**, with the
church **modes** at the side. Blues gets treated as major or minor with some "blue" notes added.
Ethan Hein argues that this is wrong. Blues has its own scales and chords, and its own rules for
how melody and chords fit together. Listeners who grew up with it hear it as consonant, not as
a set of clashes. He thinks it should be taught next to major and minor, not after them.

This series follows two sources. One is Hein's essay "Blues tonality". The other is Panos
Charalampidis's video series *Microtonal Blues Scales*, which teaches the blue notes one
degree at a time on the guitar. This first lesson sets out the main ideas. The others go
through them one at a time:

1. **A system of its own** (this page)
2. [The scales called "blues"](blues-tonality-scales.qmd)
3. [Blue notes: areas, not points](blues-tonality-blue-notes.qmd)
4. [Majorish, minorish and neutral](blues-tonality-microtonal.qmd)
5. [Blues harmony: the dominant 7th at home](blues-tonality-harmony.qmd)
6. [Mixture, harmonica, form and style](blues-tonality-beyond.qmd)

**How to use the page.** The bar at the bottom of the window sets the **Key**, the **Lead**

## Three systems, not two

Hein follows the jazz teacher Andy Jaffe, who splits Western harmony into three systems:
**diatonic** (major and minor), **modal**, and **blues**, and wants all three taught as equally
basic. Citing Lucy Green, he notes that popular musicians, who are often self-taught, already
treat blues as a core system. Like many rock guitarists, Hein learned the pentatonic and blues
scales long before the major scale.

Hein's definition is about pitch only. **Blues tonality** is a family of pitch collections that
includes blue notes. **Blues harmony** is chords whose roots come from those collections. Rhythm,
sound and the 12-bar form are left for other lessons (see [Changing the Changes](blues-changes.qmd)).

## A dominant 7th that does not need to go anywhere

In classical harmony, a dominant 7th chord (like G7 in C) is unstable. It "wants" to resolve to
the key chord. In blues, the key chord itself is a dominant 7th, and songs start and end on it.
Some never leave it. Hein's example is Willie Dixon's *Spoonful*, which is riffs over one chord.

Choose **One chord: I7** in the Backing menu and press **▶ Backing**. Listen for a minute. Does it
sound as if it has to move on? Then try **Drone** and **One chord: Im7**.

<div class="bz" data-w="chords" data-set="ending" data-title="Two endings: a blues one and a hymn one"></div>

Both endings sound finished. They are finished in two different systems.

## The 3rd that is neither

The clearest sign of blues tonality is the 3rd of the scale. A piano has a minor 3rd (♭3) and a
major 3rd (3). Blues singers and guitarists often sing or play the space between them. The
**neutral 3rd** sits halfway, about 350 cents above the key note (a semitone is 100 cents).

Start a **Drone** or **Power chord vamp**. Then press and drag along the strip, from the ♭3 key
up to the 3 key and back.

<div class="bz" data-w="zone" data-deg="3" data-title="The 3rd: drag between the piano's two 3rds"></div>

The coloured areas are a sketch made for this site from how Charalampidis describes them. They
are not measurements. [Lesson 3](blues-tonality-blue-notes.qmd) explains what has actually been
measured.
